<document>
# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

response:
# Review: Achterberg et al., "Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis"

**This is the most balanced document in the set, and the main conclusions are reasonable.** It does several things well:

- It registered the protocol before the search.
- It prefers actual hours over scheduled hours.
- It separates per-hour from per-worker output.
- It codes work type with good reliability (κ = 0.84).
- It reports a prediction interval, which is the honest summary given I² = 81%.
- Its position between the Halden pilot and the Varga & Holm comment is well calibrated: per-hour gains are real but smaller than claimed, and the model is not sector-general.

There is one clear overclaim, about duration and novelty, and several analytic points need tightening.

## Arithmetic and internal consistency

**Everything checks out.**

- The study counts add to 23 on every split: 9 + 14, 8 + 15, 13 + 7 + 3, and 12 + 11.
- Every confidence interval is symmetric on the log scale around its point estimate, as it should be for log ratios. For example, the overall estimate of 13.4% is the log-midpoint of 8.1% and 19.0%. I checked all 13 intervals, plus the trim-and-fill, duration and controlled-discretionary estimates.
- The prediction interval (−4% to +34%) is centred correctly.
- The implied fall in hours is plausible in each group:

| Group | Calculation | Implied fall in hours |
|---|---|---|
| Coverage-bound | 0.911 / 1.062 | ≈ 14% |
| Discretionary | 1.006 / 1.151 | ≈ 13% |

The overlap figures also let me reconstruct the design–measurement cross-tab:

| | Actual hours | Scheduled hours | Record-based | Manager-reported |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Controlled (9) | 6 | 3 | 7 | 2 |
| Uncontrolled (14) | 2 | 12 | 5 | 9 |

This matters for point 3 below.

## Major issues

### 1. The duration claim overreaches, and contradicts the Limitations section

The paper claims "Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside." It rests on four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, compared *between studies* with the overall estimate. That cannot support the conclusion, for four reasons.

- **Between-study comparison.** Decay is a *within-study* question: do the same organisations' gains shrink over time? Comparing long studies with short ones confounds duration with everything else that differs between them. The right analysis uses studies with repeated measurements and models the time trend within each study.
- **Survivorship.** Long follow-up usually exists only where organisations kept the schedule. Halden's reverting organisations, for instance, would not appear in a 24-month follow-up. Long-run estimates therefore select on success.
- **Design mix.** If the four long studies are disproportionately uncontrolled, or use scheduled hours, their +14.0% should be compared with the matching subgroup, not the overall figure. Report their design characteristics.
- **Precision.** The interval (+6.2% to +22.4%) is compatible with decay to around 6%, which would be substantial decay from the uncontrolled estimate.

The Limitations section itself says "Most studies are short." Replace the claim with something like: "The few long-follow-up studies do not show smaller gains, but the evidence cannot exclude decay."

This also weakens the rebuttal of Varga & Holm. Novelty was their main argument for the residual, and the paper sets it aside on this evidence.

### 2. How was the Varden trial coded?

Varden has two strata with opposite per-worker results, one discretionary and one coverage-bound. Coding it as a single study creates a problem either way.

- **Coded "mixed":** the 3 mixed studies are the two manufacturing studies plus one other, which may be Varden. If so, the strongest randomised evidence for *both* categories has been left out of both. That is especially costly for coverage-bound work, which rests on k = 7.
- **Split into two entries:** the count is no longer 23, and the two entries share a county, an analysis and a control structure. That dependence needs handling with robust variance or multilevel models.

State which approach was used. The same question applies to any other study with sub-strata, and to Halden, whose sectors span both categories.

### 3. The "convergence" in the Discussion is largely the same studies counted repeatedly

The Discussion says controlled studies, actual-hours studies, record-based studies and the bias-adjusted estimate "converge on roughly 8 to 10%." The cross-tab shows these subgroups overlap heavily. Six of the 8 actual-hours studies, and 7 of the 12 record-based studies, are controlled. The agreement therefore partly reflects one subset of studies being counted several times.

The informative estimate is the **intersection**: controlled, actual hours *and* record-based. It is probably 4–6 studies, possibly fewer. Report it, even if imprecise. That is the estimate which genuinely "avoids the problems the re-analysis identified."

### 4. The rebuttal of Varga & Holm needs the same precision

The paper says the controlled and actual-hours subgroups "avoid the problems that re-analysis identified." They avoid some of them, but not all.

- **The controlled subgroup still has measurement problems.** It includes 3 scheduled-hours studies and 2 manager-reported studies.
- **The actual-hours subgroup still has a design problem.** It includes 2 uncontrolled studies.
- **Six of the nine controlled studies are matched or difference-in-differences, not randomised.** Organisations that self-select into treatment can still differ from matched controls.
- **Novelty is not addressed** (see point 1).
- **Attrition is not addressed.** Varga & Holm showed that Halden's withdrawals were related to the outcome. How did the meta-analysis handle that, and attrition in other pilots?

The conclusion that per-hour gains are not entirely an artifact is probably still right, given the Varden case-processing stratum and the intersection estimate. It should rest on the intersection, though, not on single-moderator subgroups.

It would also help to say which Halden estimate entered the analysis. The original reported only scheduled hours. Varga & Holm's microdata supply actual hours and record-based output for subsets. Did the review use the reported 23.4%, or a corrected figure?

### 5. The small-study effect has a competing explanation

The paper reads the funnel-plot asymmetry as publication bias. A competing explanation is design heterogeneity. Small studies are probably disproportionately uncontrolled pilots using scheduled hours and manager ratings, and those features are already known to inflate estimates.

Trim-and-fill also performs poorly when heterogeneity is high (I² = 81%). It can impute "missing" studies that are really just the effect of moderators.

Suggested additions:

- Egger's test, or PET-PEESE, **with the moderators included**, to see whether asymmetry remains once design is controlled.
- Funnel asymmetry examined **within** the controlled subgroup.
- The description softened to "small-study effects, which may reflect publication bias or the design features of small studies."

Contacting the authors of known pilots partly addresses publication bias. Say how many unpublished studies that yielded.

## Smaller points

- **The meta-regression has too many parameters.** Three moderators, one with three levels, means about four parameters on k = 23. The 58% figure is unstable. The paper acknowledges this, but it should report the confidence interval or a permutation test.
- **The coverage-bound wording overstates consistency.** "Consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%)": with k = 7, I² is very imprecise. Say whether all seven point estimates are negative, if that is what "consistent" means.
- **The mechanism correlation has a wide interval.** r = 0.18 across 11 studies has a 95% CI of roughly −0.47 to +0.70. It is also a study-level (ecological) correlation. It is uninformative, not evidence of a weak link, and the text should say so.
- **The sick-leave figure has a measurement artifact.** The pooled −31% likely includes the day-counting effect: fewer scheduled days means fewer recordable sick days. Most of these studies were also uncontrolled. Flag both, or restrict to controlled studies.
- **The inclusion criteria are inconsistent.** Self-rated productivity is excluded, but manager-rated output is included, though it is also subjective and the moderator analysis shows it inflates estimates. Consider a sensitivity analysis that excludes manager-reported output entirely. The record-based subgroup partly does this.
- **The per-worker pooled estimate mixes baselines.** Controlled studies contribute a difference against controls, while uncontrolled studies contribute a change from baseline. That is standard but worth stating as a limitation, since the uncontrolled baseline absorbs secular trends.

## Suggested revisions

1. Withdraw "novelty explanations can therefore be set aside," in both the Results and the Abstract. Add within-study time-trend analyses where data allow.
2. State how Varden, Halden and other multi-stratum studies were coded.
3. Report the controlled × actual-hours × record-based intersection estimate, and base the Discussion's main figure and the Varga & Holm response on it.
4. Say which Halden estimate was used, and how attrition was handled.
5. Run small-study tests with the moderators included, and soften the publication-bias interpretation.
6. Add uncertainty to the meta-regression R² and to the mechanism correlation.

## Where the four documents now stand

| Document | Per-hour gain claimed | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Halden pilot | +23.4%, sector-general | Inflated by scheduled hours, manager ratings and survivorship |
| Varden RCT | +12.5% discretionary, +6.7% coverage | Best single source; per-worker output falls in coverage-bound work |
| Varga & Holm | "Entirely an artifact" | Good corrections, but the conclusion is unsupported |
| This meta-analysis | About 8–10% after adjustments | Well calibrated; the duration claim is the main overreach |

The meta-analysis lands close to Varden's case-processing result and to Varga & Holm's corrected 10.8%, which is reassuring. The open question it does not resolve is the one Varga & Holm raised: whether that gain persists.

I can draft revised Duration and Discussion sections if that would help.
